who: People who use symbols or icons to understand fields
takeaways: Fields that ask for information about the user, such as name, email, phone or address, are coded with their purpose.
In HTML this is the autocomplete attribute, with tokens like given-name, email, tel and postal-code.
It lets browsers and password managers fill the field, and lets assistive tools add familiar icons.
It only covers fields about the person using the form, and only purposes on the WCAG list. A search box or a gift recipient’s name is not covered.
failures: Name and address fields with autofill turned off
Wrong tokens, such as a full name field marked as given-name
One “address” box with no purpose, where the list has a fitting token
check: Mark every field in the file that asks about the user.
Fill the prototype or build with your browser’s autofill and see which fields fill correctly.
Check that split fields, like first and last name, each have their own purpose.

quiz.question: A checkout has a “Your email” field and a “Recipient’s email” field for a gift. Which need an input purpose?
options: Both, because both are email addresses
Neither, because autofill is a browser feature
quiz.why: The criterion covers information about the user. Marking the recipient field as the user’s email would also make autofill put in the wrong address.

spec: Write the autocomplete token next to each field about the user.
Note fields about other people that must not autofill with the user’s details.
Keep field splits matching real tokens, such as given-name and family-name, or one name field.
review: Which of these fields describe the person filling them in?
Did anyone try this form with autofill?
Why is autofill turned off here, and who decided?
tradeoff: Teams sometimes turn off autofill to avoid wrong entries. Use correct tokens instead. Correct tokens give good fills, and turning autofill off hurts the people who need it most.
system: Give the input component an autocomplete property, and preset it in patterns like address and contact forms.
pitch: Autofill done right means fewer keystrokes and fewer typos, and checkouts finish faster.
